Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.

Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.

WORLD PASSWORD DAY: CHECK IF YOUR PASSWORDS ARE SAFE

The story was reported by The Register and comes from Siim Kostabi, co-founder of Pageloot, a company that provides QR codes for businesses. Kostabi said his company brought in an outside contractor to help with back-end API integrations. The contractor had credentials for the company's staging environment, which is essentially a test version of its system.

The contractor wanted easy access to those credentials from multiple devices. So they put the information into a Google Doc and set the document so anyone with the link could view it. Later, a Pageloot developer was working on an unrelated problem and typed the company's domain into Google Search. Autocomplete surfaced one of the staging hostnames followed by what appeared to be a credential string.

The team checked and found the accessible Google Docs URL. The Register reported that Google Search had indexed the document and offered information from it as a search suggestion. Pageloot quickly cut off the contractor's access and rotated the exposed credentials. The company also adopted a rule against storing passwords in Google Docs, Slack or Notion and other collaboration tools.

Before you start worrying that every Google Doc you have ever created could suddenly appear in a search, there is an important piece of context. Google told CyberGuy that Google Docs are restricted by default. The person who creates the document controls how it gets shared.

Google's current Drive guidance says Restricted means only people with access can open a file. If you select Anyone with the link, anyone who gets that link can use the file without signing in to a Google Account. Google separately lists a Public setting, when available, that allows anyone to find the file through Google Search.

Google also told CyberGuy that a link to a publicly shared Doc may be indexed if someone posts that link somewhere public where a search engine crawler can find it. The Register says the Pageloot document eventually surfaced through Google Search autocomplete. However, the report does not explain how Google first discovered the Docs URL. For the rest of us, the useful lesson is simple: pay attention to the sharing setting before putting anything sensitive in a cloud document.

Kostabi also described a separate incident involving one of Pageloot's customers. The midsize retailer discovered that its QR codes had started sending shoppers to a competitor's website.

According to Kostabi, the company investigated and found that a former employee's credentials had never been revoked. He said the former employee used that lingering access to redirect the retailer's URLs. That mistake carries a very familiar lesson.

When someone no longer needs access to an account or shared file, their access should go away too. That applies at work, but it can also apply at home. Maybe you once shared a financial document with an accountant. Perhaps an old household file still includes someone who no longer needs it. Shared access can be easy to forget because the file quietly remains in Google Drive.

WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE

You do not have to run a business to learn something from this story. Plenty of people use Google Docs and Drive to keep household information, travel plans or tax documents and other details they want available across devices.

The danger comes when sensitive information lands in a file with broader access than you realize. A Google Doc can feel private because you remember sending the link to only one person. What really counts is who currently has permission to open it and what the General access setting says. That makes this a good time to check the files you would least want a stranger opening.

A few small changes can reduce the chance that an old shared file or exposed password turns into a much bigger security problem.

If you have passwords sitting in a Google Doc right now, move them to a reputable password manager. Password managers are designed to securely store logins and make them available across your devices. They can also help you create unique passwords instead of reusing the same one. Check out the best expert-reviewed password managers of 2026 at Cyberguy.com for options and what to look for. After moving a password, delete it from the document. If other people may have had access to the file, change that password too.

Start with documents containing financial information or account details.

On a computer:

Google says switching General access to Restricted means only people with access can open the file.

On iPhone, iPad or Android:

This setting can be handy when you need to share something quickly. However, anyone who gets the link can access the file without signing in to a Google Account. That link can also get forwarded or copied somewhere you never expected. For sensitive documents, share the file directly with specific people instead.

Open the sharing settings on important files and scan the list of people who can still get in. If someone no longer needs access, remove them. This is especially worth doing after you finish working with a contractor or service provider. At home, the same idea applies when you have shared a document temporarily and the reason for sharing it has passed.

Changing a Google Doc from broad access to Restricted helps close the door, but it cannot undo exposure that may have already happened. If a password was sitting in a document other people could access, change it. Then check the account's recent login or security activity for anything you do not recognize.

Two-factor authentication adds another step when someone tries to sign in to your account. That can help protect you if a password gets stolen. CyberGuy's guide to multifactor authentication apps can help you strengthen accounts that support this added protection.

Strong antivirus software adds another layer of protection on your computer and phone. It cannot fix a Google Doc with the wrong sharing setting. However, it can help detect malicious downloads, phishing attempts and other threats that may follow if criminals get hold of your login information. Keep your security software updated and make sure real-time protection stays turned on. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Identity theft protection makes the most sense when an exposed document contained more than a password. For example, you may want extra monitoring if someone gained access to your Social Security number, financial account information or other highly sensitive personal data. Identity theft protection services can watch for signs that your information is being misused. Some also alert you to suspicious activity tied to your identity. If the exposure involved only one account password, changing that password and securing the account may be enough. The level of protection you need depends on what information was actually exposed. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

You probably have old Google Drive files you have not opened in months or even years. Spend a few minutes checking the sharing settings on documents containing sensitive information. You may find an old permission you completely forgot about. For more ways to lock down cloud files, see our guide on protecting sensitive documents and controlling file access.

Google also addressed a separate privacy question with CyberGuy. The company told us that it does not use private Workspace content, including Drive and Docs, to train its foundational AI models such as Gemini. Google's published Workspace guidance likewise says Workspace data isn’t used to train or improve the underlying generative AI models that power Gemini, Search and other systems outside Workspace without permission. That issue is separate from what happened in the Pageloot story. This case centered on how the document was shared and how credentials were handled.

FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK

What gets me about this story is how ordinary the original decision probably felt. Someone needed a password on more than one device and chose an easy place to put it. That shortcut eventually left company credentials where Google Search autocomplete could surface them. The second incident carries another lesson I think all of us can use. Access should have an expiration date. When somebody no longer needs to open one of your files or accounts, remove them. I would also take five minutes today and look at the Google Docs you care about most. Check the people who can open them and look at the General access setting. You may find nothing wrong. Great. But if you uncover an old shared link or a person who should no longer have access, you will be glad you looked before somebody else did.

When was the last time you checked who can still open the Google Docs and Drive files you've shared over the years? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: Second lady Usha Vance fires back at pointed jab from Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed
item.description: Usha Vance responded to Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's remark that seemingly questioned whether JD Vance's Papaw would have accepted her Indian ethnicity.
item.content:encoded:
PROGRAMMING NOTE: Watch the exclusive interview with second lady Usha Vance Wednesday on "Fox & Friends," starting at 6am ET.

Second lady Usha Vance responded to what critics described as a "racist" dig from Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who appeared to question how Vice President JD Vance’s grandfather would have regarded her.

The exchange began after Vance criticized El-Sayed’s views on Sharia law during a rally in Ohio, arguing the practice would be completely alien to his grandfather, whom he calls his "Papaw."

"He once argued, not too long ago, that criticisms of Sharia law were rooted in White supremacy," Vance said of El-Sayed, the American-born son of Muslim Egyptian immigrants.

VANCE UNLOADS ON EL-SAYED OVER SHARIA REMARKS: ‘THAT’S NOT MY GRANDPA’S DEMOCRATIC PARTY’

"I'd love to go back in time and tell my Papaw that there is a man who claims to stand for working people who says not only should we have Sharia law, but if you criticize it, you're a White supremacist. That's not my Papaw’s Democratic Party, my friends," the vice president continued.

Responding to the vice president’s jab, El-Sayed wrote: "So do we think JD is taking Usha with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no…"

Critics interpreted the remark as an insinuation that Vance’s grandfather would not have accepted Usha because of her Indian heritage.

EL-SAYED UNDER FIRE ONLINE AFTER TAKING AIM AT USHA VANCE, FEMALE TRUMP AIDE IN WEEKEND SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS

"I have to admit, I kind of laughed," Usha Vance told "Fox & Friends" in an exclusive interview set to air Wednesday morning.

"Because yes, I never met JD's Mamaw and Papaw. But I do know and love the children that they raised, his mom, his aunt and uncle. And they have never been anything but incredibly loving."

El-Sayed further addressed the comment in an interview on Saturday.

"The confusing thing about it is that he thinks that there are some people who are more American than others because they can point to their Papaw who was here earlier," he told MS NOW. "And my question to him is simply: Why is it then, how do you look your parents-in-law in the eye and say that somehow they're less American than you are? Because that's what he's implying there."

JD was raised in large part by his grandparents, James and Bonnie Vance, who he calls his "Papaw" and "Mamaw." James died in 1997 and Bonnie died eight years later.

Usha and JD met while attending Yale Law School and married in 2014. Although she never met her husband's late grandparents, the mother of four said her husband’s aunt has become a "second mother" to her.

"His aunt is like a second mother to me," said the second lady. "And so I have to think that if they raised children like that, they would have been loving as well. And I would have really, really, really loved to have met them."

In his 2016 memoir, "Hillbilly Elegy," Vance wrote that one of his "great regrets" was that his grandparents never had the opportunity to meet his wife.

El-Sayed’s campaign did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

item.title: Dolly Parton dead at 80
item.description: Dolly Parton, country music legend, has died after months of battling unknown health issues. Her nephew announced the news in a video posted to her Instagram page.
item.content:encoded:
Legendary country singer and songwriter Dolly Parton has died. She was 80. 

Parton died peacefully in Nashville, Tennessee on Tuesday, according to a press release obtained by Fox News Digital. 

Her nephew revealed the news in an Aug. 25 Instagram video. The news comes after Parton spent months battling an unknown health issue.

DOLLY PARTON ADMITS HUSBAND CARL DEAN'S DEATH HAS BEEN 'BIG ADJUSTMENT' AFTER 60-YEAR ROMANCE

"My name is Brin Seaver, son of Cassie Parton, and I’m representing the Parton and Owens family today announcing the passing of my aunt, Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean, Sister, Sis and Granny to one generation and Gigi to the next," he says in the video. "This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality. As her head of security for more than two decades, a role my father Larry held before me, I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it until now."

"It is an honor, an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness. But sadness lies with us, not with Dolly. Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by Carl, her parents and countless others who have watched her and longed to meet her in the heavens."

"I first went on the road with Dolly as a kid, getting a taste of the road life in the early 1980s. Dolly opened doors not just for me, but for her entire family to reach the potential we didn’t even know was possible. Dolly also opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent," Seaver added in the video message. "By her example, we believed that anything is possible. She never saw a door she couldn’t open, and the doors she opened made and changed history."

"My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you," Seaver continued. "She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family whether you liked it or not. Our family and the team she has entrusted with her legacy will work diligently to ensure her spirit will live with us forever. Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy; he farmed the soil, she farmed songs and happiness. Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because, after a life of wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest."

"Rest in peace, Aunt Dolly — Aunt, Granny, Gigi. May God bless Dolly Parton, and may God bless you all. She will always love you."

Born in 1946 in rural Sevier County, Tennessee, Parton grew up in a large, poor family in the Smoky Mountains. She began singing in church as a child, started writing songs at a young age and moved to Nashville after graduating high school to pursue music.

Her breakthrough came as a performer on "The Porter Wagoner Show," where she became a fan favorite before forging a solo path that would establish her as one of country music’s most prolific and influential songwriters.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I’ll always be a country musician because I’m a country girl," she told People in 1975. "My style is my soul and my feelings. I’ll tell the world in my songs what I wouldn’t have told my mother."

Parton’s catalog included enduring hits such as "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," "Here You Come Again," "9 to 5" and "I Will Always Love You." The latter song became a global phenomenon again when Whitney Houston recorded it for 1992’s "The Bodyguard."

DOLLY PARTON UNABLE TO WRITE NEW SONGS AFTER LOSING HUSBAND OF NEARLY 60 YEARS

Parton made her feature film debut opposite Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin in 1980’s "9 to 5." Parton later appeared in films including "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas," "Rhinestone," "Steel Magnolias" and "Joyful Noise."

Parton was also known for her decades-long marriage to Carl Dean, who largely stayed out of the public eye during their nearly 60 years together. Dean died in March 2025.

After Dean died at the age of 82, the "Jolene" singer explained why she couldn't get herself to do what she loved: write songs. 

"I can’t afford the luxury of, you know, getting that emotional right now," she said during an appearance on Khloé Kardashian’s podcast, "Khloé in Wonder Land." "There are times like that, things like that, that will stall you a little bit. But I’ll write something else though, if it comes."

"I’m just putting that all on hold," Parton said. 

In November of that same year, the country music legend opened up about her impressive career spanning more than seven decades, got candid about the personal sacrifices she's made throughout the years and explained why she feels like she's "just getting started."

"You know, I have just been going so fast my whole life," Parton told People at the time. "And I just start thinking, ‘How in the world did I even have a life? How did I even get it done?’ I really realized when I was putting this book together just how much I had sacrificed in my life. I never had children, so at least I didn’t have a guilty feeling. I’m thankful that I got to see my dreams come true."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"People say, ‘Well, you’re going to be 80 years old.’ Well, so what? Look at all I’ve done in 80 years. I feel like I’m just getting started," said Parton. "I know that sounds stupid, but unless my health gives way, which right now I seem to be doing fine… I think there’s a lot to be said about age. If you allow yourself to get old, you will. I say, ‘I ain’t got time to get old!’ I ain’t got time to dwell on that. That’s not what I’m thinking about."

Parton has battled various health issues over the past couple of years. 

In May, the country legend announced she was canceling her planned Las Vegas residency, which had already been postponed from 2025 to September 2026 because of health concerns.

Earlier this month, Parton missed a major Dollywood event per doctor's orders. 

"I’m still in Nashville, and I’m sorry about that," Parton told the crowd during a video appearance at the event, according to video shared by the Knoxville News Sentinel.

"I’m supposed to be there in person, like we planned," she continued. "Now I’ve told you before, all my fans, that I have had a few little health issues. And sometimes I get a little dizzy, and I get dehydrated."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"And I’m dehydrated," Parton, who appeared on-screen wearing fairy wings, told the crowd. "And, so, my Nashville doctor clipped my wings, saying, 'You ain’t traveling this week.’"

Parton had previously discussed problems involving kidney stones, saying her immune and digestive systems had gotten "out of whack" and were being treated. 

Beyond her impressive career, Parton built a business empire centered in her home state of Tennessee. Dollywood became one of Tennessee’s most popular attractions, while her charitable work through the Dollywood Foundation and Imagination Library left an equally lasting mark.

The Imagination Library, which sends free books to children from birth until kindergarten, was inspired by Parton’s father, who never learned to read or write. The program grew into an international literacy initiative and distributed millions of books to families around the world.

"With heavy hearts, the Dollywood family mourns the passing of our beloved Dreamer-in-Chief, Dolly Parton. Everyone at Dollywood shares the sorrow of countless people around the world touched by Dolly’s warmth, wisdom and generous spirit," a representative from Dollywood said in a statement. 

"Dolly’s heartfelt wish was that Dollywood always remain a place of joy, hope and togetherness—a space where families and friends could honor her memory, not with silence, but with laughter, music and shared dreams."

"Dolly’s enduring legacy extends beyond her music and generosity to her remarkable work ethic—an inspiration to people everywhere. In her spirit, Dollywood will be open Wednesday as Dolly wanted, always reminding everyone with her signature sparkle — 'the show must go on.' Together, we honor her by carrying forward her message of love, perseverance, and hope."

At Parton’s request, a small, private service will be held for immediate family.

item.title: GOP's Singer 'very prepared' to oust Dem Moskowitz in toss-up Florida race that could determine House majority
item.description: Scott Singer says Florida's redrawn 25th Congressional District gives Republicans a path to flip Jared Moskowitz's seat in a narrowly divided House.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., a self-described moderate, is facing political headwinds in the race for the newly-redrawn 25th Congressional District in South Florida, as Republican nominee Scott Singer sees a path to pick up a House seat in a narrowly divided Congress.

"We're going to be very prepared to go flip this seat – it is a key targeted seat," Singer told Fox News Digital in an interview Monday.

"This is a key district that may determine the balance of power in the House."

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME

The race is drawing national attention and, potentially, big Democratic dollars to defend the seat in Democrats' pursuit of the majority to attack what House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries just called the "cartel" of President Donald Trump.

"A lot of people in this district and beyond understand what's at stake here," Singer, former Boca Raton mayor, said.

Moskowitz, currently seated in the more Democratic-friendly 23rd District, is – like Singer – Jewish and pro-Israel, but he will have to navigate a tougher Republican-friendly map and fend off the "anti-Israel wing" of the Democratic Party, according to to Singer.

FLORIDA DEMOCRAT SENDS 'CONDOLENCES' TO HASAN PIKER AFTER DEFEATING DSA CHALLENGER IN FLORIDA PRIMARY

"His voting record speaks volumes," Singer said. "Since he's gotten to Congress, he's been locked up with the Democrats on almost every issue."

"This is not the sort of record of bipartisanship he once had. He's been much more partisan because he has to be," Singer claimed. "He has to appeal to a more far-left socialist led Democratic Party if he's going to have any influence. And that's going home to roost in November."

When reached for comment, the two-term Moskowitz stressed he fought off the Democratic Socialists of America's maximum pressure campaign in his primary, while keeping $2 million cash on hand for the general election and expecting "we'll have the national resources" in the fight to keep the seat blue.

"I go after my party all the time and fight within," Moskowitz, who was twice appointed to positions by Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis in a show of bipartisanship, told Fox News Digital, noting Singer has been "awfully silent" on social media amid his own vocal defense against the "anti-Israel" political factions.

FROM WASSERMAN SCHULTZ TO GOLDMAN, DEMOCRATIC INCUMBENTS ARE FIGHTING FOR SURVIVAL

"Scott just has talking points, which is why he's the masked singer. You hear a voice behind a mask. He says things to all sorts of people, tells people what they want to hear, but nobody really knows where he stands because he never really takes positions."

The heated rhetoric belies a previously tighter relationship.

"Scott Singer endorsed me when I ran the first time," Moskowitz claimed.

Singer's campaign has denied it was anything more than a personal call to generally express support for a fellow Jewish, pro-Israel politician.

Singer, though, says he is well-positioned in the newly redrawn South Florida district, with a growing GOP voter-registration advantage and Democratic division working against the "quasi-incumbent."

"People are abandoning the Democratic Party because the mainstream Democratic Party of even a few years ago has abandoned them," Singer said. "It's now a socialist-led party and it's sad for America."

"That's why we need to band together and make sure independent voters understand what's at stake," he added. "We can't have people talking about communism or new Democrat-incoming members of the House saying horrific things like that they would wipe their hand on the American flag if they didn't have a napkin. That's today's Democratic Party, unfortunately, and it's not something I want to see."

MOSKOWITZ REJECTS RICK SCOTT'S CLAIMS HE'S 'SCARED TO DEATH' OF SOCIALISTS, BEHOLDEN TO HASAN PIKER

The race is considered to be one of 19 toss-ups in the nation (seats held by four Democrats and 15 Republicans), according to the Cook Political Report.

"It's now about five points more Republican than Democrat, but even since redistricting, there are Republicans who are registering at a higher rate: People in Florida have seen the success of our state and seen the craziness other places, and they're voting more conservative," Singer said.

"And we have a great opportunity to pick off disaffected Democrats who are sick with the socialist lean, especially in our community that has a large number of residents who fled communism, like my family, like wife's family did," he continued. "They understand that bringing socialism and communism into the United States is a terrible idea. That's another reason why we're optimistic about our chances to flip this must-win seat in November."

DESANTIS UNDER PRESSURE AS FLORIDA REDRAW COULD TIP HOUSE BALANCE IN GOP MAP FIGHT

The race also presents an unusual political dynamic: Singer and Moskowitz are both Jewish candidates competing in a district where roughly a quarter of the electorate is Jewish, one of the highest concentrations in the country.

"The anti-Israel wing, which has taken root in the Democratic Party, is doing the convincing for us," Singer said. "Because we've seen a majority of House members would deny arms sales to Israel, our ally during a time of conflict.

"And that's the party, where it is. We've seen three incumbents in the Democratic Party ousted in recent months solely because Israel was the key issue.

"Anti-Israel is winning. It's become the mainstream of the Democratic Party. And longtime Democrats are leaving in droves. Another reason why it's going to be very hard for Democrats in this district to win with 25% Jewish population and people who understand Israel's close and long-standing alliance with the United States. We're going to pick off more of those voters."

5 TAKEAWAYS FROM FLORIDA SENATE PRIMARY: GOP SEN. ASHLEY MOODY WILL FACE DSA'S NIXON

Also, while GOP-leaning, the district is still largely independent. It snakes along South Florida's Atlantic coast through portions of Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade counties, encompassing communities around Delray Beach, Boca Raton, Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood and Miami Beach.

"I was already running under the prior boundaries when it leaned Democratic, but I'm thrilled with the new boundaries because it runs from Miami Beach, where I was born, through Fort Lauderdale where I grew up, through Boca Raton where I served as mayor for eight years," Singer said.

"I have deep ties in this district. It's my whole life. I've lived 40-plus years in this District in all three counties. My opponent doesn't live in the district. I'm not sure he's ever lived in the district. And I think those community ties help when you're trying to represent 750,000-plus people."

Moskowitz lives in nearby Parkland and was born and raised in Coral Springs, which is just west of the newly drawn district, which carved those towns out.

FLA DEM SEN-NOMINEE ANGIE NIXON BACKED ABOLISHING ELECTORAL COLLEGE, RANKED-CHOICE VOTING IN RESURFACED CLIPS

Trump would have carried the territory by roughly nine points in 2024 after Joe Biden would have won it by about five points in 2020, showing just how the district is turning conservative and more favorable to flip.

"Jewish voters don't just have to vote for a Jewish candidate who may be not terrible on Israel ... now you have a pro-Israel, Zionist candidate who's a strong Republican who will vote for the common sense solutions: We need like less regulation, lower taxes, insurance reform and more."

"Independent voters have a choice," he added. "Are we going to continue on tax reform, secure borders, economic improvement... or are we going to go back to what the Democrats would propose, which frankly for the next two years is just impeachment?

"Nothing will get done in Washington," he concluded.

item.title: Dangerous debris washes ashore before beachgoer makes another troubling find
item.description: A Jersey Shore beachgoer says she found more needle plungers and drug paraphernalia the day after Manasquan Beach reopened following a syringe cleanup.
item.content:encoded:
A popular Jersey Shore beach reopened to swimmers after dozens of syringes washed ashore — only for a beachgoer to report finding more concerning debris along the sand the following day.

The syringes and paraphernalia were discovered littered across the sands of Manasquan Beach in Manasquan, along the Jersey Shore, on Saturday.

Officials at the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) said the debris included household waste, including syringes used for at-home insulin injections, according to local outlets.

DANGEROUS WATER WARNINGS HIT TRENDY VACATION SPOT AFTER POWERFUL STORM POUNDS AREA

Mayor Michael Mangan told Fox News Digital the syringes were first discovered Saturday afternoon and were cleaned up and properly cleared away. 

"There was a large amount of additional debris, indicating a garbage spill of some kind, and the incident was localized to the south end beach, along the Manasquan Inlet jetty," Mangan said.

It's believed the debris washed ashore following recent heavy rainfall and sewer overflows, according to local reports citing the NJDEP.

Mangan added that, in accordance with guidance from the NJDEP and Monmouth County health officials, the town waited for two high-tide cycles, which occurred overnight Saturday.

SUMMER TRAVELERS WARNED AFTER FECAL BACTERIA LEVELS IN WATER EXCEED SAFETY STANDARDS

By 9 a.m. Sunday, state and local officials "met on site, and no syringes were observed — so the water was reopened," Mangan told Fox News Digital.

But not all residents agreed with the timing of reopening the waters.

Priscilla Mahajan, a Manasquan resident, told local outlet News 12 she found needle plungers and drug paraphernalia on Sunday.

Mahajan had participated in the cleanup efforts the day before. She said she felt the beach reopened too soon.

"One beach cleanup is definitely not enough to say something is safe," the resident said.

Mahajan added, "We can't change what's in the ocean or what people have done in the past, but we can change our reaction to it."

Mahajan told CBS News she found syringes, cut straws, syringe plungers, syringe caps and small plastic baggies along the beach.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Fox News Digital reached out to the NJDEP, but the agency declined to comment.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The syringe discovery comes less than two weeks after another unusual scene unfolded along the Jersey Shore, when nearly 30 dead juvenile dogfish sharks were found scattered across a beach in Sea Isle City.

At the time, shark ecologist Mike Heithaus told Fox News Digital that seeing so many sharks wash ashore at one time was rare.

The incident did not appear consistent with a widespread toxin or pollution event, Heithaus said, and he suggested the sharks may have been caught and discarded.

item.title: US military plane lands in Moscow, with Kremlin claiming it has no information: report
item.description: A video has emerged showing a U.S. military C-17A Globemaster III aircraft approaching for a landing at Moscow, Russia's Vnukovo airport on Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
Video captured a U.S. military transport plane coming in for a landing Tuesday at Moscow's Vnukovo airport, in a flight that the Kremlin reportedly claimed it had no information about.

Data from the website Flightradar24 showed that the Boeing C-17A Globemaster III left Joint Base Andrews in Maryland early Sunday afternoon on a flight to Riga, Latvia. The aircraft then traveled from Riga to Moscow, Russia on Wednesday morning.

The last time a U.S.-registered jet made a direct flight to Russia from Europe was in January when special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, visited Moscow for a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin about the war in Ukraine, according to Reuters.

A Department of War spokesperson told Fox News Digital on Tuesday, "We have nothing to provide on this subject." Fox News Digital also has reached out to the White House and the U.S. Embassy in Moscow for comment.

PUTIN 'PANICKED' AS DEFIANT UKRAINE MARKS INDEPENDENCE DAY UNDER RUSSIAN BOMBARDMENT

The Kremlin said it had no information about the latest flight, Reuters reported.

Yury Ushakov, an aide to Putin, said following January’s meeting with Witkoff and Kushner that "our counterparts arrived from Davos after taking part in a series of events together with President Donald Trump, including those concerning the Ukraine settlement."

MARINE VETERAN ROBERT GILMAN RETURNS TO US SOIL AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION FULFILLS REQUEST: 'NO AMERICAN LEFT BEHIND'

"They offered what can be called their first-hand accounts of these events and shared their impressions, as well as their latest thoughts and assessments regarding the meeting between the President of the United States and [Ukraine President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy in Davos" during the World Economic Forum, he added.

"Overall, I can say that the focus of the meeting between the President of Russia and US representatives was to obtain information resulting from the contacts the United States had with the Ukrainians and Europeans in order to define further steps between our two countries," Ushakov also said.
